# Cūḷasaccaka Sutta (MN 35 (PTS MN i 227))
**ID:** MN 35 (PTS MN i 227)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Cūḷasaccaka Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse With Saccaka", MN 35) is the thirty-fifth discourse of the Majjhimanikāya, set in the Mahāvana forest outside Vesālī [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In this discourse, Saccaka, the son of Nigaṇṭha (Jain) parents who is addressed by the clan name Aggivessana, boasts of his skill as a debater and challenges the Buddha to a philosophical contest [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Galasek 2016; Jamspal 1991]. Saccaka asserts that the five aggregates (*khandha*) constitute the permanent self (*attā* / *ātman*) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Jamspal 1991]. The Buddha systematically refutes this position by demonstrating that the aggregates are impermanent (*anicca*), unsatisfactory (*dukkha*), and outside autonomous control, thereby establishing the teaching of not-self (*anattā*) [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. During the debate, King Ajātasattu is cited as an example of monarchical authority [Radich 2011], and the Buddha remarks on his ability to sit motionless for days experiencing supreme bliss [Polak 2011]. When Saccaka twice refuses to respond to a question, he is compelled to answer under the threat of the yakkha Vajirapāṇī shattering his head [Gergely, Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī; Galasek 2016]. Following his defeat, Saccaka hosts the Buddha and the monastic community for a meal [Jamspal 1991]. The sutta is also referenced in several debates of the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 1.1, Kv 2.8, Kv 23.5) [SuttaCentral].
Full parallels to the discourse are preserved in the Chinese Āgamas (*Saṁyukta-āgama* SĀ 110 and *Ekottarika-āgama* EĀ 37.10), Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 34), and the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (Up 6.005) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2014]. DharmaNexus confirms extensive cross-language alignment with the Chinese *Saṁyukta-āgama* (T 99) and *Ekottarika-āgama* (T 125), the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Dharmaskandha*, and the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (D 4094) [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali Canon, DharmaNexus identifies significant text-reuse with the Khandha Saṁyutta (SN 22), the Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta (SN 35), the Vinaya Khandhakas (Kd 1 and Kd 6), and discourses sharing doctrinal pericopes or dramatic narrative elements, such as the *Upāli Sutta* (MN 56) and the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3) [DharmaNexus; Gergely, Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī].
